cdbg.description: Provides annual grants on a formula basis to states, cities, and counties to develop viable urban communities by providing decent housing and a suitable living environment, and by expanding economic opportunities, principally for low- and moderate-income persons. The program is designed to reinforce flexibility, consolidated planning, and technical assistance to build community capacity.
eligible_activities: acquisition of real property
relocation and demolition
rehabilitation of residential and non-residential structures
construction of public facilities and improvements
public services
energy conservation and renewable energy resources
assistance to profit-motivated businesses for economic development
resident_input_opportunities: Consolidated Plan public hearings
Annual Action Plan public comment periods
citizen participation in local government meetings
community needs assessment input
cdbg.leverage_point: Residents can influence funding allocation through participation in consolidated planning process, public comment periods, and by contacting local municipal or county officials who determine which local projects receive funding

home_investment_partnerships_program.administering_agency: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)
home_investment_partnerships_program.description: Provides formula-based grants to states and localities to create affordable housing for low-income households. HOME funds can be used for a wide range of activities including building, buying, or rehabilitating affordable housing for rent or homeownership, or providing direct rental assistance to low-income people.
eligible_activities: Acquisition, construction, or rehabilitation of affordable rental housing[1][2][3].
Assistance to homebuyers for purchase and/or rehabilitation of homes[1][2][3].
Tenant-based rental assistance (TBRA) for low-income households[1][2][3].
Rehabilitation of owner-occupied housing to improve safety, accessibility, and energy efficiency[1][3].
Development of transitional and permanent housing for individuals and families experiencing or at risk of homelessness[4].
Support for Community Housing Development Organizations (CHDOs) to develop affordable housing[3][5].
Accessibility modifications for persons with disabilities[1][3].
resident_input_opportunities: Public hearings and comment periods: Local governments must hold at least one public hearing and provide a public comment period (typically 30 days) during the development of the Consolidated Plan and Annual Action Plan[1][3].
Community needs assessment: The planning process must include an assessment of local housing and community development needs, with opportunities for residents to provide input[1][3].

Resident advisory committees or councils: While not mandatory, many jurisdictions establish advisory committees or councils to ensure ongoing resident input, especially from low-income and minority populations[1].
Annual planning and reporting: The Annual Action Plan and Consolidated Annual Performance and Evaluation Report (CAPER) both require public review and comment before submission to HUD[1][3].
home_investment_partnerships_program.leverage_point: Participation in public hearings and comment periods during the development of the Consolidated Plan, Annual Action Plan, and CAPER. Engagement in community needs assessments by attending meetings, responding to surveys, or submitting written comments.

section_8_housing_choice_voucher_program.administering_agency: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), implemented by local Public Housing Agencies (PHAs)
section_8_housing_choice_voucher_program.description: The Section 8 HCVP is a federally funded rental assistance program that helps low-income families, seniors, and individuals with disabilities afford safe, decent housing in the private market[1][2]. HUD provides funding and oversight, but local implementation is managed by Public Housing Agencies (PHAs), which determine eligibility, issue vouchers, inspect units, and pay subsidies directly to landlords on behalf of tenants[1][2]. PHAs also maintain waiting lists, conduct outreach, and ensure compliance with federal regulations.
eligible_activities: Issuing tenant-based vouchers that allow eligible households to choose and lease privately owned housing (apartments, single-family homes, townhouses) that meets program standards[1][2][3].
Administering project-based vouchers tied to specific housing developments, increasing the stock of affordable units in targeted neighborhoods[1][3].
Providing mobility counseling to help voucher holders access neighborhoods with greater opportunities (schools, jobs, services)[1].
Supporting homelessness prevention by prioritizing vouchers for individuals and families experiencing or at risk of homelessness (as allowed by local preferences)[1].
Ensuring housing accessibility by working with landlords to modify units for people with disabilities and prioritizing accessible units in project-based developments[3].
Conducting outreach and education to landlords and tenants about program rules, rights, and responsibilities[2].
Collaborating with local service providers to connect voucher holders with supportive services (e.g., job training, childcare, health care)[1].
resident_input_opportunities: Public hearings on PHA plans and policies
Resident advisory boards at local PHAs
Annual public comment periods on PHA Annual Plan
section_8_housing_choice_voucher_program.leverage_point: Participate in public hearings and comment periods on PHA Annual Plans and policies. Advocate for voucher allocation priorities and mobility programs that expand housing opportunities.

low_income_housing_tax_credit_lihtc_prog.administering_agency: Internal Revenue Service (IRS) under the U.S. Department of the Treasury
low_income_housing_tax_credit_lihtc_prog.description: The LIHTC program provides federal tax credits to state housing agencies, which then allocate these credits to private developers for the construction or rehabilitation of affordable rental housing[1][2][3]. Local governments often participate by supporting projects through zoning, infrastructure, gap financing, or by collaborating with state agencies to identify community needs and priorities for affordable housing development[2][3].
eligible_activities: New construction of affordable rental housing for low- and moderate-income households[1][2].
Rehabilitation of existing rental housing to preserve or improve affordable units[1][2].
Acquisition and preservation of at-risk affordable housing to prevent loss of existing affordable stock[1][2].
Supportive housing development for populations experiencing homelessness or with special needs (when paired with other funding sources)[3].
Accessibility improvements to ensure compliance with ADA and fair housing requirements[3].
Site improvements and infrastructure upgrades necessary for affordable housing development (often with local or state funds in conjunction with LIHTC)[2].
Mixed-income or mixed-use developments that include a required percentage of affordable units[2].
resident_input_opportunities: Public hearings and comment periods: State housing agencies must hold public hearings and provide opportunities for public comment on their QAP, which sets priorities and selection criteria for LIHTC awards[3].
Community needs assessment: The QAP process typically involves an assessment of local and statewide affordable housing needs, often informed by public input[3].
Resident advisory committees/councils: Some states or localities may establish advisory groups to provide input on housing priorities, though this is not federally mandated for LIHTC[3].

Annual planning/reporting with public input: Updates to the QAP and related planning documents generally require public notice and comment periods, allowing residents to influence priorities for LIHTC allocations[3].
low_income_housing_tax_credit_lihtc_prog.leverage_point: Participate in public hearings or comment periods during the QAP development or amendment process at the state housing agency. Submit written comments or attend meetings when local governments or housing authorities discuss affordable housing priorities or support for specific LIHTC projects.

emergency_solutions_grants.administering_agency: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), Office of Community Planning and Development
emergency_solutions_grants.description: Provides federal funding for rapid re-housing, homelessness prevention, emergency shelter, and street outreach services. ESG helps communities engage homeless individuals and families living on the street, improve the number and quality of emergency shelters, help operate these shelters, provide essential services to shelter residents, rapidly re-house homeless individuals and families, and prevent families and individuals from becoming homeless.
eligible_activities: Emergency shelter operations, essential services, and renovation
Street outreach to unsheltered homeless individuals
Rapid re-housing assistance including rental assistance and housing relocation
Homelessness prevention including rental assistance and housing stabilization services
Data collection and HMIS participation
Administrative costs for program administration
resident_input_opportunities: Consolidated Plan public hearings and comment periods
Annual Action Plan development with required citizen participation
Continuum of Care coordination meetings
Community needs assessment input sessions
emergency_solutions_grants.leverage_point: Participate in Consolidated Plan public hearings and Continuum of Care coordination meetings. Advocate for specific homelessness services or populations. Engage with local ESG subrecipient organizations to influence service delivery priorities.

housing_opportunities_for_persons_with_a.program_name: Housing Opportunities for Persons with AIDS (HOPWA)
housing_opportunities_for_persons_with_a.administering_agency: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), Office of Community Planning and Development
housing_opportunities_for_persons_with_a.description: The only federal program dedicated to addressing the housing needs of persons living with HIV/AIDS. HOPWA provides housing assistance and related supportive services to help individuals with HIV/AIDS and their families establish or maintain stable housing, reduce risk of homelessness, and improve access to HIV treatment and other health care support.
eligible_activities: Tenant-based rental assistance (TBRA) for persons with HIV/AIDS
Short-term rent, mortgage, and utility payments to prevent homelessness
Facility-based housing including community residences and single-room occupancy dwellings
Permanent housing placement services
Supportive services including case management, substance abuse treatment, and mental health services
Housing information and resource identification
Operating costs for housing facilities
resident_input_opportunities: Consolidated Plan public hearings and comment periods
Annual Action Plan citizen participation process
HIV/AIDS housing planning councils and advisory committees
Community input sessions on HOPWA funding priorities
housing_opportunities_for_persons_with_a.leverage_point: Participate in Consolidated Plan public hearings and local HIV/AIDS housing planning processes. Engage with HOPWA project sponsors and advocacy organizations to influence housing assistance priorities and service delivery models.

housing_trust_fund.administering_agency: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), Office of Affordable Housing Programs
housing_trust_fund.description: Provides grants to states to produce and preserve affordable housing for extremely low-income (ELI) households, including homeless families. The HTF targets households at or below 30% of area median income (AMI), with priority given to projects that serve the lowest income households for the longest period of time and leverage other funding sources.
eligible_activities: Production of new rental housing for extremely low-income households
Preservation and rehabilitation of existing affordable rental housing
Construction of permanent supportive housing for homeless populations
Operating cost assistance and operating cost reserves for HTF rental units
Reasonable and necessary administrative and planning costs
resident_input_opportunities: State allocation plan public hearings and comment periods
Consolidated Plan citizen participation process
Local affordable housing development project review processes
Public comment on state HTF allocation priorities
housing_trust_fund.leverage_point: Participate in state allocation plan hearings and comment periods. Advocate for HTF funding in your community by engaging with state housing finance agencies. Support local developers applying for HTF funds through letters of support and community testimony.

continuum_of_care.administering_agency: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), Office of Special Needs Assistance Programs
continuum_of_care.description: Provides funding to local continuums of care for projects that provide housing and services to individuals and families experiencing homelessness. The program promotes community-wide commitment to ending homelessness through coordinated entry systems, evidence-based practices, and performance measurement. CoC funds support permanent supportive housing, rapid re-housing, transitional housing, and supportive services.
eligible_activities: Permanent supportive housing for chronically homeless individuals and families
Rapid re-housing to help homeless individuals and families quickly exit shelter
Transitional housing with supportive services
Supportive services only for persons in permanent housing
Homeless Management Information System (HMIS) data collection and analysis
Coordinated entry system development and operation
Planning and administration for CoC activities
resident_input_opportunities: CoC board and committee meetings open to public participation
Annual Point-in-Time count volunteer opportunities
Coordinated entry system community input processes
CoC application priority setting public meetings
Homeless services provider coordination meetings
continuum_of_care.leverage_point: Join your local Continuum of Care board or committees. Participate in annual Point-in-Time counts and community planning processes. Advocate for specific populations or service models during CoC application priority setting. Engage with homeless service providers to influence local homeless system design.
